headline: Highest risk is data leakage: oh-my-openagent has broad egress and shared workspace surfaces, while langchain4j is local-only but can still be fed sensitive content through files and prompts.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: oh-my-openagent exposes runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and file surfaces, so it can ingest content from shared files or tool outputs; langchain4j is a local library with no egress, but if its outputs are passed into oh-my-openagent, prompt-like content can be reinterpreted. The pathway exists in default-style integrations, though not proven directly.
conditions: IF both agents are connected through a shared workspace or copied transcripts
IF oh-my-openagent parses langchain4j-generated text as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces
Disable automatic ingestion of generated text into prompts
Add a provenance tag to all inter-agent handoffs
Review any MCP hook that reads files before enabling it
requires-engineering: enforce instruction/data boundary checks

B_data_leakage.rationale: oh-my-openagent has broad network egress, browser, and subprocess capability plus touches provider auth data and session history; langchain4j has no egress, but it can still be used to prepare sensitive content that oh-my-openagent may transmit. The pair creates a default leakage path if they share files or prompts, even though the exact bridge is not documented.
conditions: IF sensitive prompts, session history, or provider auth data are available to oh-my-openagent
IF langchain4j-generated content is forwarded into oh-my-openagent without redaction
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared files and prompts
Turn off browser and API egress where possible
Use separate OS users for each agent
Redact auth material before any handoff
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction at the transfer boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: langchain4j is a library with no write surfaces shown, while oh-my-openagent writes to multiple config and cache paths and supports multiple instances. If both are used in the same project tree or config area, overlapping writes can corrupt state or overwrite agent settings; uncertainty about the exact shared path pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same config, cache, or project directory
IF multiple oh-my-openagent instances run against one shared installation
mitigations: Assign separate config directories
Run only one writer per workspace
Back up config files before changes
Use file locks around shared state
requires-engineering: add transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: oh-my-openagent includes team messaging/task APIs and LSP actions, so it can act on upstream text; if langchain4j output is treated as authoritative, errors can cascade into messages, tasks, or code edits. langchain4j itself is not an action agent, but it can still supply the content that oh-my-openagent operationalizes.
conditions: IF langchain4j output is forwarded into team_send_message, team_task_create, or LSP actions
IF oh-my-openagent does not verify the upstream text before acting
mitigations: Require human review before task creation
Add a verification step for all imported text
Limit LSP write actions to dry-run mode
Log source provenance on every action
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating before execution

E_compliance.rationale: oh-my-openagent touches anonymous telemetry, installation identifiers, session history, and provider auth prompts, while langchain4j is documented only as a local open-source library with no data classes touched. The mismatch is mainly on the oh-my-openagent side; if regulated data enters its telemetry or history paths, compliance risk arises even though langchain4j itself is not the residency driver.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is entered into oh-my-openagent session history or telemetry paths
IF provider auth prompts are logged or retained beyond policy
mitigations: Disable telemetry if allowed
Avoid placing regulated data in session history
Review retention settings for logs and caches
Separate auth prompts from project content
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
